title: What should you ask first in a competitive response case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a competitive response case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first how big the threat is in revenue and profit terms, because the right response to a rival's move depends on how much of the client's business is really at risk. The trap is never comparing your proposed response with doing nothing, which is often cheaper than it looks.
body:
The first question to ask

How big is the threat: which customers, how much revenue and how much margin are at risk?

When a rival cuts prices or launches a product, clients tend to react to the headline. Sizing the exposure calms the case down. A discounter attacking 10% of the client's customers calls for a narrow, targeted response; one attacking the core calls for something bigger. Ask what the rival has done, in which segments, and whether the client has lost any sales yet.

How to build your structure

  • Exposure: customers, revenue and margin at risk.
  • The rival's motive: which segments it targets, and whether it can keep this up.
  • Options: do nothing, defend current customers, respond on price or product, partner or buy.
  • Choose: on profit impact, cost, speed and risk, each compared with doing nothing.

The full tree is in the competitive response framework. To judge how strong the rival's position is, Porter's five forces helps.

Worked response: a rival undercuts by 20%

A coffee brand sells 1 million packs a year at $5, with a variable cost of $3 a pack. Contribution is $2 a pack, or $2M a year. A rival launches at $4 and management wants to match it at once.

OptionVolumeContribution per packTotal
Match at $4, keep every customer1,000,000$1$1.0M
Hold at $5, lose 20% of volume800,000$2$1.6M
Match only in the 30% of sales in discount stores300,000 + 700,000$1 and $2$1.7M

Matching halves contribution even in the best case, where no customer leaves. Holding price beats matching unless volume falls by more than half (below 500,000 packs, $2 × 500,000 = $1M). A targeted response, here matching only where shoppers are price-sensitive, can beat both, as long as the cheaper price does not spread to other stores.

The numbers are illustrative; the logic is the point. Find out who would actually switch, and where. Ask whether the rival can sustain a $4 price or is buying share for a few months. Consider other options too: a loyalty offer for the most exposed shoppers, a smaller pack at a lower shelf price, or a stronger case for why the product is worth $5. Then think about how retailers and the rival will react to each move.

The trap most people fall into

Not comparing with doing nothing. Every response costs money, and many cost more than the sales they protect.

Weak: "We should match the price immediately so we don't lose customers."
Strong: "Matching everywhere costs $1M of contribution even if we keep every customer. Holding price only does worse if we lose more than half our volume. I'd hold, and match selectively in discount stores where shoppers are most likely to switch."

Two prompts to try

A low-cost airline has launched on your client's most profitable route.

Show the answer
  • Exposure: share of the client's route profit from leisure versus business travellers.
  • Rival: its fares, frequency and costs; whether the route is profitable for it.
  • Options: hold, fare-match on some seats, add frequency, protect corporate contracts.
  • Choose: profit under each, compared with doing nothing.

Where to start: exposure by segment. Business travellers who value timings and flexibility may not switch at all.

The trap: a fare war on every seat when only leisure passengers are at risk.

A competitor has launched a free version of software your client sells.

Show the answer
  • Exposure: which customers could manage with the free features; their revenue share.
  • Rival's motive: win users and upsell to paid plans; can it fund this for long?
  • Options: hold; launch a limited free tier; add features the free version lacks; lock in renewals.
  • Choose: revenue at risk against the cost of each response.

Where to start: exposure. Small customers using basic features are at risk; larger ones with integrations and switching costs often are not.

The trap: launching a free tier that downgrades your own paying customers.
